# 1 Overview

We'll now look at the dplyr verbs corresponding to each operator in Codd's relational algebra.
As a running example, we'll use the nycflights13 dataset.
This dataset contains information about all flights that departed from New York City (e.g. EWR, JFK and LGA) to destinations in the United States, Puerto Rico, and the American Virgin Islands in 2013: 336,776 flights in total.
To help understand what causes delays, it also includes a number of other useful datasets:

- `flights`: all flights that departed from NYC in 2013
- `weather`: hourly meterological data for each airport
- `planes`: construction information about each plane
- `airports`: airport names and locations
- `airlines`: translation between two letter carrier codes and names

## 1.1 Starting a Spark Session

First we need to start a Spark session in local mode. We also ensure the nycflights13 package is installed and loaded.

```{r}
library(sparklyr)
library(dplyr)

spark_disconnect_all()

conf <- spark_config()
conf[["spark.env.SPARK_LOCAL_IP.local"]] <- "0.0.0.0"
conf[["spark.driver.host"]] <- "127.0.0.1"
conf[["spark.ui.port"]] <- 4040

sc <- spark_connect(
  master = "local[2]",
  spark_home = "/opt/spark/spark-3.4.0-bin-hadoop3",
  version = "3.4.0",
  hadoop_version = "3",
  config = conf
)

spark_connection_is_open(sc)

if (!"nycflights13" %in% rownames(installed.packages())) {
  install.packages("nycflights13")
}
library(nycflights13)
```

We can now load the data from our local R session into Spark. We'll use the `sparklyr::copy_to()` function, which copies data frames into Spark tables on our spark session:

```{r}
flights_tbl <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, nycflights13::flights, "flights", overwrite = TRUE)
airlines_tbl <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, nycflights13::airlines, "airlines", overwrite = TRUE)
airports_tbl <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, nycflights13::airports, "airports", overwrite = TRUE)
planes_tbl <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, nycflights13::planes, "planes", overwrite = TRUE)
weather_tbl <- sparklyr::copy_to(sc, nycflights13::weather, "weather", overwrite = TRUE)
```

# 2 Selection Verbs (\(\sigma\))

The relational algebra selection operator \(\sigma\) corresponds to the `filter()` verb in dplyr. It selects rows that satisfy a given predicate (similar to the filter function on RDDs):

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  filter(origin == "JFK", month == 1, day == 1) %>%
  head() %>%
  collect()
```

All dplyr operations on a Spark DataFrame are translated into SQL queries that Spark can execute. We can view the SQL generated for a dplyr verb using `show_query()` as follows:

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  filter(origin == "JFK", month == 1, day == 1) %>%
  show_query()
```

# 3 Projection Verbs (\(\pi\))

The relational algebra projection operator \(\pi\) corresponds to the `select()` verb in dplyr (unfortunate naming, I know...).

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  select(year, month, day, carrier, flight, tailnum, dep_delay, arr_delay) %>%
  head() %>%
  collect()
```

We can also see the SQL generated by dbplyr for the select operation:

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  select(year, month, day, carrier, flight, tailnum, dep_delay, arr_delay) %>%
  show_query()
```

# 4 Union Verbs (U)

The relational algebra union operator U corresponds to the `union()` verb in dplyr:

```{r}
jfk_jan <- flights_tbl %>%
  filter(origin == "JFK", month == 1) %>%
  select(year, month, day, flight)

jfk_feb <- flights_tbl %>%
  filter(origin == "JFK", month == 2) %>%
  select(year, month, day, flight)

jfk_union <- union(jfk_jan, jfk_feb)
jfk_union %>%
  count() %>%
  collect()
```

```{r}
union(jfk_jan, jfk_feb) %>%
  show_query()
```

You can also use `union_all()` to keep duplicates:

```{r}
union_all(jfk_jan, jfk_feb) %>%
  count() %>%
  collect()
```

# 5 Difference Verbs (-)

Set difference corresponds to the `setdiff()` verb in dplyr:

```{r}
jan_all <- flights_tbl %>%
  filter(month == 1) %>%
  select(year, month, day, flight)

feb_all <- flights_tbl %>%
  filter(month == 2) %>%
  select(year, month, day, flight)

only_in_jan <- setdiff(jan_all, feb_all)
only_in_jan %>%
  count() %>%
  collect()
```

```{r}
setdiff(jan_all, feb_all) %>%
  show_query()
```

# 6 Join Verbs (\(\bowtie\))

The inner join operator \(\bowtie\) corresponds to the `inner_join()` verb in dplyr:

```{r}
joined <- flights_tbl %>%
  inner_join(airlines_tbl, by = "carrier") %>%
  select(year:day, carrier, name, flight, tailnum)

joined %>%
  head() %>%
  collect()
```

```{r}
joined %>%
  show_query()
```

# 7 Rename Verbs (\(\rho\))

We can rename columns using `rename()`, which corresponds to the relational algebra rename operator \(\rho\):

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  rename(departure_delay = dep_delay, arrival_delay = arr_delay) %>%
  select(year:day, departure_delay, arrival_delay) %>%
  head() %>%
  collect()
```

# 8 Aggregation Verbs (\(\gamma\))

The relational algebra aggregation operator \(\gamma\) corresponds to `group_by()` combined with `summarize()` in dplyr.
`group_by()` partitions the data by one or more columns.
`summarize()` computes aggregate statistics (mean, sum, count, etc.) for each group.

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  group_by(carrier) %>%
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(count)) %>%
  collect()
```

# 9 Duplicate Elimination Verbs (\(\delta\))

The relational algebra duplicate elimination operator \(\delta\) corresponds to `distinct()` in dplyr. `distinct()` removes duplicate rows, optionally keeping only specified columns. Without arguments, it removes completely identical rows. With column arguments, it keeps only unique combinations of those columns.

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  distinct(origin, dest) %>%
  arrange(origin, dest) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  collect()
```

# 10 Sorting Verbs (\(\tau\))

The relational algebra sorting operator \(\tau\) corresponds to `arrange()` in dplyr. `arrange()` orders rows by one or more columns in ascending order by default. Use `desc()` to sort in descending order. Multiple columns create hierarchical sorting (first by column 1, then by column 2, etc.)

```{r}
flights_tbl %>%
  select(year, month, day, carrier, dep_delay, arr_delay) %>%
  arrange(desc(dep_delay)) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  collect()
```
